text: A trained policy isn't evidence of anything until it's checked on episodes it never saw during training. This lesson builds that held-out grid, runs the trained policy against it, and compares it to SQL Server's own default plan on the exact same episodes.

The held-out grid uses two hundred forty date range and territory combinations, sampled with a seed never used during training, spanning the same range as training did: one day to three years, across all available territories. Evaluation checks the policy's most likely action, not a stochastic sample, to measure what it actually settled on.

Across those two hundred forty held-out episodes, the agent's chosen hint matched or beat the optimizer's own default plan on seventy eight percent of them, a clear majority. On the episodes where it won outright, the average logical-read reduction was thirty four percent relative to the optimizer's default.

The result isn't clean everywhere, though. The losses cluster in one place: date ranges roughly between ten and eighteen days, right at the narrow to wide transition the Lesson 1 notebook entry was originally probing. In that boundary zone, the agent still picks force order on a meaningful share of episodes and loses to the optimizer's default when it does — a real boundary case regression, not a rounding error.
